paragraphs.heading: Magnitude and intensity
paragraphs.text: A seismic magnitude scale describes how strong, or how big, an earthquake is overall. Magnitude is an estimate of that relative size, and so of the potential of the earthquake to shake the ground. Intensity is a different thing. It is the strength of the shaking at one given place.

paragraphs.heading: Where the shaking comes from
paragraphs.text: Tectonic forces put the crust of the Earth under stress. Sometimes the stress grows large enough to break the crust, or to beat the friction that stops one block of crust slipping past another. Energy is then released. Some of it takes the form of seismic waves of various kinds, and these waves cause the ground to shake.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the waves
paragraphs.text: Magnitudes are usually worked out from seismic waves as recorded on a seismogram. An earthquake sends out different kinds of seismic waves, and their characteristics reflect both the rupture and the crust they pass through. Finding a magnitude generally means picking out specific kinds of waves on the seismogram and then measuring one or more features of a wave, such as its timing, amplitude, frequency or duration. Further adjustments are made for distance, for the kind of crust, and for the characteristics of the seismograph that made the recording.

paragraphs.heading: Richter and his zero point
paragraphs.text: The first scale for earthquake magnitudes was developed in 1935 by Charles F. Richter. It is popularly called the "Richter" scale, but it is actually the local magnitude scale, labelled M_L. Richter established two features that all magnitude scales share. One is that the scale is logarithmic. The other is the zero point, which he defined arbitrarily: it is set where an earthquake 100 km away produces, on a seismogram from a Wood-Anderson torsion seismograph, a largest horizontal displacement of 0.001 mm.

paragraphs.heading: Why one scale is not enough
paragraphs.text: Most magnitude scales rest on measurements of only part of the seismic wave-train of an earthquake, so they are incomplete. In certain cases this leads to a systematic underestimate of magnitude, a condition called saturation. The original "Richter" scale was developed in the geological setting of Southern California and Nevada. For earthquakes in central and eastern North America it later turned out to be inaccurate, because the continental crust there is different.

paragraphs.heading: Soft ground far from the source
paragraphs.text: How hard the ground shakes locally depends on several factors besides magnitude, and soil conditions are among the most important. Soft soil in thick layers, fill for example, can make seismic waves stronger, and this often happens a long way from the source. Sedimentary basins will often resonate, which makes the shaking last longer. This is why, in the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake, San Francisco's Marina district was among the areas with the most damage, even though the epicenter was nearly 100 km away.

paragraphs.heading: What gets reported
paragraphs.text: For earthquakes above magnitude 4.0, most seismological authorities report the moment magnitude, M_w. The United States Geological Survey is one example. The press describes this figure as "Richter magnitude". All magnitude scales keep the logarithmic scale that Richter devised, and they are adjusted so that the middle of their range roughly matches the original "Richter" scale.
